cue_frames.expected_caption: Open Workflows in the Chicago Fire demonstration department.
We will build a training call-created workflow with two ordered actions
and a separate call-closed workflow.
Begin with the outcome you want and the event that should cause it.
Each workflow listens to one event.
Multiple steps can respond to that event, while a different
event needs a different workflow.
Inspect the list's event and enabled columns before editing,
and identify who will monitor the result when the automation runs.
Open Credentials and create Academy local captured mail.
Choose SMTP Email.
In this isolated exercise, Mailpit receives messages inside
the training network; nothing goes to an outside mail service.
Set the local host, port and demonstration sender, keep the
unused password masked, and save.
Your live department needs its own mail provider settings and
appropriate transport security.
The credential type must match the action.
A stored credential supplies authentication details; it does
not establish that a destination is reachable or accepts a message.
Choose New Workflow and name it Academy call opened — captured mail.
Select CallAdded as Trigger Event.
Turn Enabled off while configuring the destination and actions,
and review the retry controls.
The event becomes fixed after creation, so confirm it before saving.
Keep retry values modest for practice and observe actual attempt timing later.
Template gallery examples also need their destinations and credentials
completed before enabling.
A descriptive name makes the event and operational purpose easier to
recognize in the workflow list.
Select Add Step.
Choose Send Email and set Order to one.
Enter the fictional training-supervisor address and a subject, then
select Academy local captured mail as the SMTP credential.
In Output Template, use a short training message with department name and call
name from the variable reference.
Keep unnecessary personal details and narratives out of the message.
Save the step and inspect its card in the editor.
The card shows the action and a template excerpt; the execution history will
show whether a send actually completed.
Add a second Send Email step at Order two.
For this exercise, run it only when the call name contains TRAINING.
Use Visual Builder for simple comparisons, or Raw Expression with Scriban braces.
Here, call.name
piped to string.contains
TRAINING must render true for the step to run.
Select Test Condition and read the result carefully.
A syntax-valid message means the expression can be read; without
sample event data, it does not establish whether this call will pass.
Save the condition with the step, then inspect the actual run later to
confirm whether it ran or skipped.
Create Academy call closed — captured mail as a second workflow, choose CallClosed,
and add its own closeout action.
Keep it disabled until checked.
This gives each event a visible definition and history.
It does not make the first workflow wait for the second event.
For other operations, choose the actual available event, such as
a unit status change, completed checklist or finalized record.
Check the event's timing and data before choosing template variables.
Ordered steps belong to the event that started that specific run.
Reopen Academy call opened — captured mail and review the destination,
credential, enabled steps and order.
Confirm the training receiver and background processing are ready.
Enable the workflow and save.
Create one approved training call whose name contains TRAINING.
That operational event is the execution test.
If the action is meant for email, a file store or a messaging
platform, use a controlled test destination for that service.
Do not infer a working integration merely from the workflow's enabled
badge or the absence of a form error.
Open Runs for the workflow, then open the training run.
Read its status, attempt number, start and completion times.
Inspect each step's log and duration, including the conditional step.
Expand Rendered Output when your permissions allow it and compare the
actual message with the template.
A skipped step should have an understandable reason; a failed step
needs its recorded error reviewed.
Compare the receiver's own controlled receipt when you need proof of delivery,
because a workflow log alone may describe only the action's handoff.
Open Health to review recent successful, failed and skipped runs and performance.
Use the different time windows to see whether a single
failure is part of a pattern.
Pending Runs shows work that is waiting, running or retrying.
Inspect a run before using Cancel, and understand what Clear Pending will affect.
These controls manage queued work; they do not undo an action already
accepted by another service.
Keep the run identifier when investigating, so the workflow, event and
destination evidence remain connected.
For a controlled retry exercise, pause only the isolated training receiver
and trigger a fresh close event.
In this example the same run reaches three attempts, then fails with
Maximum retry attempts exceeded.
Read the SMTP error in its step logs.
Restoring the receiver does not restart an exhausted run.
A fresh training close event creates a different run, which completes on
attempt one and arrives in the receiver.
Retries happen automatically; this page does not provide a general Retry button.
Earlier actions can run again, so destinations must
tolerate duplicate attempts.
In this build, the saved thirty-second backoff did not match the observed
five- and ten-second gaps, so confirm timing in the run history.
Finally, disable the training workflows and keep their run history.
These controls also fit community care and mental health teams, search
and rescue organizations, security departments, wildland contractors
and industrial response teams.
Choose the operational event and the minimum information your own process
needs; for example, route a site incident to a supervisor or a completed readiness
check to a training coordinator.
